title: The Compiègne offering
hookLine: before the danger came, a convent offered itself for peace

lines: A PROPOSAL IN A QUIET ROOM.
cards: Giving your life for something before anyone has asked for it. Not in a crisis, with no time to think, but calmly, with time to be afraid.
This path has already met the Carmelites of Compiègne at the end of their story, singing on the way to the guillotine in the French Revolution.
Today goes back earlier, to a quiet room in their convent, and a proposal that came first. The ending reads differently because of it. Today, the Compiègne offering.

teach.b: As the Revolution grew violent, the prioress, Mother Teresa of Saint Augustine, suggested something to her community: that they offer themselves to God as a sacrifice, so that peace might return to France and to the Church.
Not a protest. Not an escape plan. An offering.
Second, the fear. Tradition says not everyone agreed at once.
Some of the older sisters were frightened by the idea, and said so. The prioress didn't force them.
In time, the account goes, they joined of their own accord, and the community renewed the offering together, again and again, as part of their prayer. Third, the root.

teach.h: A LIVING SACRIFICE, DAY BY DAY.
teach.b: Saint Paul writes to the Romans, in the Douay-Rheims: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God, your reasonable service."
For a long time, a living sacrifice meant ordinary days handed over in prayer. Only at the very end did it mean the scaffold. Fourth, the peace.
Jesus says in the Beatitudes: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." The sisters couldn't stop a revolution. They had no armies, no votes, no voice in Paris.
What they had was themselves, and they gave that, for a peace they would not live to see. Catholics honor them as martyrs, and tradition says the Terror ended soon after their deaths.
Whatever you make of that, the shape is clear: a small, hidden gift, offered for something far larger than the one giving it.

how: Catholics honor the Carmelite Martyrs of Compiègne as saints, and some make a daily offering of their prayers, work and sufferings for peace, in the spirit of the sisters' act of offering.

games.q: you're an older sister at Compiègne. your prioress proposes offering your lives to God for peace, and you're frightened. what do you do?
o: say yes at once, and hide the fear.
say you're afraid, and take your time.
games.why: tradition says some sisters were afraid and said so. the prioress didn't force them, and in time they joined freely.

practice: Look at the rest of today, the commute, the work, the dinner, the tiredness, and name one place that needs peace: a country at war, a family at odds, your own street.
Gather up the day, dull parts too, and hold it out toward that place. If you pray, offer it to God for that peace, as the sisters did; if you don't, dedicate the day to it in your heart.

wordCard.voice: The Compiègne offering. The Carmelites of Compiègne giving their lives to God, long before the scaffold, for peace in France and the Church. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: peacemakers, literally peace-makers, from the Beatitudes in Matthew 5:9.

carryVoice: Your line: an offering for peace. The week ran through a table of sinners, roses, a soul with guests, a cross known by living, a joyful girl, a kitchen Carmel, each a life offered. That closes the week.
